records.name: Santander
records.summary:
No Santander-specific law, enforcement practice or incident finding for trans people appears in the record's surviving sources. The national picture they document frames what a visitor stands under anywhere in the country: an English-language report (April 2025) covered the killing of Sara Millerey, a trans woman beaten and thrown into a creek in Bello, Antioquia while bystanders filmed, whose death prompted vigils in several cities and a presidential order to investigate, a local LGBTQ council describing it as the third such killing there that year, with 13 trans people killed nationally in the first quarter of 2025; an investigation (July 2024) documented armed groups in Caquetá circulating 'social cleansing' flyers naming 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as targets, giving a trans woman a week to leave town, and recording more than 40 trans women killed nationally the previous year.

Those reported cases concern other departments; nothing in the record marks Santander as materially safer or more dangerous than that national picture. Because the documented killings and threats surface where journalists and monitors operate, the absence of Santander-specific findings is weak evidence of safety, not proof of it.

records.name: Risaralda
records.summary:
Risaralda carries no local statute aimed at trans people and no department-level incident entry in the audited record; what a trans visitor stands under is Colombia's national pattern. That pattern is violent and largely unpunished: armed groups circulated "social cleansing" flyers naming trans women as targets in 2024, at least 41 trans women were killed nationally in 2023 and 13 more in the first quarter of 2025, and of 155 criminal investigations into LGBTQ killings only 3 reached a verdict last year — roughly 2% against a 9% overall homicide-conviction rate.

State response to this violence is episodic rather than structural: the audited record shows a presidential order to investigate after a viral April 2025 murder of a trans woman in another department, vigils, and nothing resembling standing local protection machinery. Outside the largest cities the national figures are the operative risk for a visitor here.

records.name: Putumayo
records.summary:
Putumayo is a frontier department, but the audited record documents no department-specific statute, enforcement practice or incident for trans visitors: the frontier "public order" regime and displacement episodes in this record's own sources belong to Caquetá, not here, and are not claimed for Putumayo. What applies is the national picture: armed groups in several regions have circulated "social cleansing" threats against trans women (2024), at least 41 trans women were killed nationally in 2023 and 13 in Q1 2025, and conviction rates in anti-LGBTQ killings run near 2% against 9% for homicides overall.

For a visitor, that means the country-wide combination — armed-group social control in parts of the periphery, near-total impunity, episodic central-government response — rather than any documented local mechanism.

records.name: Nariño
records.summary: No department-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding was located for this division; the 2025 national reporting flags it neither for a public-order regime nor for territorial expansion of anti-LGBTIQ+ violence. It otherwise inherits national conditions.

records.name: Guaviare
records.summary:
Guaviare has no regional statute or incident entry specific to trans visitors in the audited record; the national conditions are what a visitor encounters. Those national conditions are severe in their own right: an "As Equals" investigation documents armed groups posting flyers with kill-lists threatening "homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans" (one northern department, March 2024), nearly 50 queer and trans people killed nationally in 2025 to the date of reporting, and only 3 of 155 investigations into LGBTQ killings producing verdicts — about a 2% conviction rate against 9% for homicides generally. The same reporting traces "social cleansing" campaigns and gang enforcement of social order, including expulsion of gay and trans residents.

There is no documented local protective machinery; the risk profile for Guaviare is the national pattern plus the thin institutional reach characteristic of the country's small periphery departments.

records.name: Guainía
records.summary: This department lies in the country's frontier 'orden publico' belt, where armed groups rather than departmental police effectively regulate conduct; regional reporting documents trans women displaced from frontier departments because of their gender identity, amid territorial expansion of anti-LGBTIQ violence nationally (one LGBTIQ+ person killed every 32 hours in 2025, 63% up on 2024). No department-specific legal or enforcement deviation beyond national homicide counts; risk assessed on the national framework.

records.name: Arauca
records.summary:
Arauca's own local situation for trans visitors is not established in the audited record — the frontier "public order" characterisation attached to it previously appears in no cited source, and a widely quoted per-32-hours killing statistic belongs to other compilations, so neither is repeated here. What is sourced is national: the killing of a trans woman in Antioquia (April 2025) that prompted a presidential investigation order; 13 trans people killed nationally in Q1 2025 and 41 trans women in 2023; and armed groups circulating "social cleansing" threats in at least one department (Caquetá, 2024). Impunity for anti-LGBTQ killings is near-total nationally.

Treated honestly, that means a visitor to Arauca faces the national pattern — high lethality, very low conviction, episodic state response — with no department-specific aggravation or protection on the record.

records.name: Boyacá
records.summary: No department-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding was located beyond the national homicide counts; risk assessed on the national framework.
